content: Terpin hydrate is a pharmacological agent classified as an expectorant. It is primarily utilized to facilitate the loosening and clearance of mucus in conditions such as acute and chronic bronchitis, as well as other related respiratory disorders. This compound is derived from natural sources, including oil of turpentine, oregano, thyme, and eucalyptus. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) withdrew its approval for terpin hydrate in the 1990s due to insufficient evidence supporting its efficacy. History The physiological properties of terpin hydrate were first studied by Lépine in 1855. He observed that the compound exerted effects on the mucous membranes and the nervous system, resembling the actions of oil of turpentine. By 1907, several formulations of terpin hydrate were available in the United States, as documented in the 19th edition of The Dispensatory of the United States of America. These formulations included: Elixir of Terpin Hydrate Elixir of Terpin Hydrate with Codeine Elixir of Terpin Hydrate with Heroin Uses Terpin hydrate was commonly prescribed as an expectorant for the treatment of acute and chronic bronchitis. It was often combined with other agents, such as codeine, to enhance its therapeutic effects. Pharmacologic Mechanisms of Action Terpin hydrate functions as both a humectant and an expectorant. It acts directly on the secretory cells of the bronchial mucosa in the lower respiratory tract, promoting the liquefaction and subsequent elimination of bronchial secretions. Additionally, it exhibits a mild antiseptic effect on the pulmonary parenchyma. Indications The clinical indications for terpin hydrate included: Acute and chronic bronchitis Pneumonia Bronchiectasis Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) Infectious and inflammatory diseases of the upper respiratory tract Dosage and Administration The recommended dosage of terpin hydrate ranged from 85 to 170 milligrams, administered three to four times daily. Adverse Reactions The use of terpin hydrate was associated with several adverse effects, including: Respiratory depression Sedation Impairment of motor coordination Constipation Urinary retention Prolonged use of preparations containing terpin hydrate, particularly those combined with codeine, could lead to drug dependence, specifically codeine dependence. The high alcohol content of terpin hydrate formulations (approximately 42%) also posed risks, as excessive consumption could result in significant central nervous system (CNS) depression. Current Status of Expectorants in the USA As of now, guaifenesin (glycerol guaiacolate) is the only expectorant approved by the FDA for use in the United States. Previously utilized expectorants, such as ammonium chloride, beechwood creosote, benzoin preparations, camphor, eucalyptus oil, iodine-based compounds, ipecac syrup, menthol, pine tar preparations, potassium guaiacolsulfonate, sodium citrate, squill preparations, terpin hydrate, tolu, and turpentine oil, are no longer approved and would require reformulation to meet current regulatory standards.
